papers.title: Heterotopic expression of respiratory-associated genes suggests a developmental basis for pleopodal gill evolution in isopod crustaceans
papers.abstract: Background The evolution of organs in new anatomical positions contributes to morphological diversity and offers opportunities to examine developmental evolution. Crustacean gills provide a useful comparison: isopods bear pleopodal gills on abdominal appendages, whereas many other crustaceans possess thoracic epipodal gills. Here, we combined comparative anatomy and multiplex in situ hybridization chain reaction to examine embryonic expression of the respiratory-associated genes trachealess (trh) and ventral veins lacking (vvl) in the aquatic isopod Gnorimosphaeroma cf. hoestlandti and the terrestrial isopod Porcellio scaber. We also examined the posterior Hox genes abdominal-A and Abdominal-B (AbdB) to assess regional pleonal patterning. Results In both species, trh and vvl expression occurred in developing pleopodal regions corresponding to gill-bearing tissues. In G. cf. hoestlandti, prominent expression extended into both endopodal and exopodal regions of pleopods 4-5, whereas in P. scaber, it was concentrated in the endopods of pleopods 3-5. In both species, trh showed more restricted posterior pleopodal expression than vvl, and posterior expression domains overlapped spatially with AbdB-expressing regions. Conclusions Compared with thoracic epipodal expression reported in other crustaceans, these patterns differ at two anatomical levels: along the body axis (thorax versus pleon) and among appendage structures (epipods versus endopods/exopods). These differences suggest that the acquisition of heterotopic trh and vvl expression in isopod pleopods may have contributed to the evolution of pleopodal gills. Moreover, the different expression patterns in the two isopods suggest subsequent evolutionary changes in the spatial distribution of these genes, potentially associated with the diversification of pleopodal gills.

papers.title: Comparative larval single-cell transcriptomics provides insights into the evolutionary origins of sensory-neural programmes in Porifera and Cnidaria
papers.abstract: Understanding how specialised cell types emerged and diversified is fundamental to reconstructing animal evolution. The origins of neural and sensory-secretory cell types are particularly intriguing, and early diverging non-neuronal metazoans, such as sponges, provide critical insights into pre-neural molecular toolkits. Free-swimming larval stages of sponges and cnidarians provide an unique context for investigating these questions, as these larvae rely on specialised sensory and signalling systems to detect environmental cues and coordinate behaviour during dispersal and settlement. Here, we integrated larval single-cell transcriptomic datasets from the demosponge Amphimedon queenslandica and four cnidarian species (Nematostella vectensis, Astroides calycularis, Pocillopora acuta and Clytia hemisphaerica). Cross-species mapping using Self-Assembling Manifold mapping (SAMap) recovered broad conservation of major cell-type identities among cnidarians, including neural, secretory, cnidocyte, epithelial, gastrodermal and apical populations. Extending these comparisons to A. queenslandica displayed transcriptional similarities between several sponge larval cell populations and cnidarian neural, sensory and progenitor-associated cell types. Within-species analyses showed that these cell populations remained transcriptionally integrated within the broader epithelial and sensory cell type of the sponge larva. Neural-associated gene modules, including conserved families associated with photoreception, neural fate specification and postsynaptic scaffolding, were distributed across distinct epithelial and sensory-like sponge larval cell populations rather than being restricted to a single proto-neural cell type. Our findings suggest that molecular components subsequently incorporated into neural systems were already deployed across diverse cell types in a common ancestor of sponges & cnidarians. Our work supports an evolutionary scenario in which extant neural and sensory-secretory cell types arose through the diversification and reorganisation of molecular programmes distributed across multiple ancestral sensory-secretory cell types.

papers.title: Donor-associated variation outweighs PMOS status in patient-derived iPSC transcriptomes: a genotyped, BMI-adjusted study of 14 lines
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from patients have been little used to model polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS, formerly polycystic ovary syndrome, PCOS), and differences between unrelated donors can masquerade as disease effects. Earlier comparisons of three or four donors per group reported hundreds to thousands of differentially expressed genes. We asked whether a disease signature is detectable in a larger, genotyped panel, balanced for BMI category and BMI-adjusted, of full-phenotype patients. Methods: We studied 14 clonal, transgene-free iPSC lines reprogrammed by CRISPR activation from endometrial stromal fibroblasts of seven women with PMOS meeting all three Rotterdam criteria, and seven controls frequency-matched for BMI category ( 30 kg/m2). Bulk RNA-seq (16,489 expressed genes) was related to diagnosis, hormones, metabolic traits, age, and X-inactive specific transcript (XIST) status using gene-wise models, exact enumeration of all 3,432 group splits, and permutation-calibrated gene-set tests. Donors were genotyped within a cohort of 140 women and scored with an imputation-based genome-wide PMOS polygenic risk score (PRS). PMOS risk-locus genes were examined against a 202-line iPSC proteome. Results: PMOS donors had higher anti-Mullerian hormone (AMH), testosterone, and free androgen index than controls. No gene was differentially expressed between PMOS and control lines (false discovery rate < 0.1), and the number of nominally associated genes was no greater than for random 7-versus-7 splits of the lines (p = 0.75). This was unchanged with an alternative read quantification and with count-based models. With seven donors per group, the design could detect 1.8-fold differences per gene, compared with roughly 3- to 6-fold for the three- or four-donor designs used previously. Neither diagnosis nor any hormonal or metabolic trait explained more expression variance than chance, and neither PMOS GWAS-locus genes nor Hallmark pathways were enriched. Two control lines showed near-complete loss of XIST, potentially indicative of X-chromosome inactivation (XCI) erosion, and a third was borderline. Endocrine PMOS-locus genes (e.g., FSHR, AMH) were not expressed, whereas DNA-repair and growth genes were. Across 129 genotyped women, the PRS was higher in PMOS (odds ratio 1.81 per SD; AUC 0.65), but PMOS and control iPSC donors overlapped fully in polygenic risk. Conclusions: In this panel of 14 undifferentiated iPSC lines from women with the full PMOS phenotype, no robust PMOS-associated transcriptomic differences were detected. Expression variation was dominated by line-to-line differences, consistent with donor background as their main source, although with one clone per donor a contribution of clonal variation cannot be excluded. Reduced XIST expression in some control lines is potentially indicative of, but does not establish, X-chromosome inactivation erosion. Disease-associated differences in differentiated, hormone-responsive cells cannot be excluded, and differences reported in smaller panels may partly reflect inter-donor variability. Future studies should use adequately sized panels, control for XIST erosion, select donors by polygenic risk, and examine hormone-responsive derivatives. Keywords: polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome; polycystic ovary syndrome; induced pluripotent stem cells; transcriptome; polygenic risk; XIST erosion; disease modelling; experimental design

papers.title: Matrix Gla Protein deficiency reveals a previously unrecognized mucosal calcification in the mouse airways
papers.abstract: Tracheal calcification is a common finding that is considered to have limited clinical significance when detected most often in elderly individuals. Despite its frequent occurrence, the cellular and molecular mechanisms at the origin of tracheal calcification remain largely unexplored. In this context, we aimed to characterize the development of tracheal calcification, and to determine the role of matrix Gla protein (MGP), a major inhibitor of ectopic calcification whose genetic or pharmacologic deficiency is associated with premature tracheal calcification in humans. We found that wild-type mice undergo an unexpected early physiologic calcification of the tracheal cartilage rings beginning around one month after birth. This calcification progresses in a dynamic rostro-caudal sequence through a process involving terminal differentiation of tracheal chondrocytes. These findings challenge the prevailing view that tracheal cartilage is a permanent hyaline cartilage and instead reveals an early and highly organized physiologic calcification process. Furthermore, our findings further identify MGP as a key regulator of calcification within the respiratory tract. Indeed, MGP deficiency not only markedly accelerates tracheal cartilage calcification through a similar pattern and mechanism but also induces a previously unrecognized calcification of the tracheal mucosa, a lesion absent in wild-type mice. These alterations could partly explain the respiratory manifestations observed in MGP-deficient patients having Keutel syndrome, which include dyspnea, cough, stridor, and recurrent infections, symptoms previously being mainly attributed to calcification of the tracheal cartilage rings.

papers.title: Epigenetic Mechanisms Inhibit Smad7 and Contribute to Fibrosis in Crohn's Disease
papers.abstract: Background & Aims: TGF-beta1 is a central regulator of profibrotic gene expression, extracellular matrix deposition, and the development of intestinal fibrosis in patients with fibrostenotic Crohns disease (CD). Unlike the increased expression of Smad7 in mucosal and lamina propria monocytes, where it impairs Treg function, mesenchymal cells from patients with fibrostenotic CD do not exhibit elevated Smad7 expression and instead display sustained TGF-beta1 signaling. We therefore sought to elucidate the mechanisms underlying the unexpected silencing of Smad7 in fibrostenotic CD. Methods: Subepithelial myofibroblasts (SEMFs) and muscularis smooth muscle cells were isolated from paired normal and affected ileal tissues obtained from the same patients with each Montreal phenotype of CD, as well as from non-CD controls. Gene expression, RNA-binding affinity, transcriptional activity, promoter methylation, protein levels, and the mechanisms that regulate Smad7 expression were evaluated in ex vivo tissues and primary cultured cells. MicroRNA-21 (miR-21) localization was assessed by RNAscope. miR-21-mediated suppression of Smad7 was investigated using antagomiR-21. Smad7 silencing through promoter hypermethylation was confirmed using 5-Azacytidine treatment and DNA methyltransferase 1 (DNMT1) knockdown. Smad7 lysine acetylation and Smurf1/2-mediated ubiquitination were examined using selective inhibitors and proximity ligation assays. Results: In SEMFs from patients with fibrostenotic CD, aberrant silencing of Smad7 resulted from DNMT1-dependent promoter hypermethylation and pSmad3-driven, miR-21-mediated degradation of Smad7 mRNA. In addition, Smurf1/2 promoted ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of acetylated Smad7 protein. Inhibition of miR-21 with antagomiR-21 restored Smad7 expression and reduced TGF-beta 1-dependent profibrotic gene expression. Likewise, demethylation with 5-Azacytidine or knockdown of DNMT1 induced Smad7 promoter hypomethylation and restored Smad7 expression. Furthermore, modulation of the balance between p300 acetyltransferase and histone deacetylase 1 (HDAC1) stabilized Smad7 protein by protecting it from degradation. Conclusions: A distinctive pattern of epigenetic silencing and post-translational regulation of Smad7 was identified in patients with fibrostenotic CD. These mechanisms collectively promote unrestrained TGF-beta1 signaling by suppressing Smad7 expression and stability in SEMFs, thereby contributing to the development of intestinal fibrosis.

papers.title: Northern palsa and peat ecosystem microbiomes are potentially supported by hydrogen and carbon monoxide metabolism
papers.abstract: Northern peatland and permafrost ecosystems are facing rapid changes, with increasing temperatures, permafrost thaw and shifts in hydrology. Characterizing microbial communities and metabolic potential from the soils and associated water bodies is crucial to understanding the changes in biogeochemical cycling in these ecosystems. For this, samples were collected and sequenced from subarctic palsa and peat soils, along with samples from associated thaw ponds and streams. Metagenomics was utilized in describing the microbiome and its metabolic potential in these environments. Palsa soils hosted microbial communities that were distinct from the peatland soils, ponds and stream waters. Soils and their adjacent ponds shared taxa, and peat soils and ponds also shared taxa with the streams, unlike palsa soils which were likely more hydrologically isolated. Based on metabolic marker gene ratio for denitrification [(nirS+nirK)/nosZ], palsa soils had the strongest potential to be a source of nitrous oxide (N2O) out of all the sample types. Marker genes for hydrogen gas (H2) and carbon monoxide (CO) utilization were abundant across soil environments and metagenome assembled genomes, suggesting that trace gas oxidation is likely one of the key energy sources for microbiomes. In the palsa ponds and peat soils pmoA, marker gene for methanotrophy, was the most abundant compared to the other sample types.

papers.title: Gene-resolved metagenomics reveals partitioned nitrogen transformation potential in a landfill leachate sequencing batch reactor microbiome
papers.abstract: Landfill leachate can contain high concentrations of ammonia and organic nitrogen requiring treatment before discharge. Sequencing batch reactors (SBRs) promote biological nitrogen removal through alternating aerobic and anoxic conditions, but taxonomic profiling alone cannot resolve how nitrogen transformation and competing retention pathways are distributed across microbial communities. This study applied gene-resolved metagenomics to a sludge sample collected from a UK landfill leachate SBR. Nitrogen-metabolism genes were linked to contig-level taxonomic assignments and metagenome-assembled genome bins to examine nitrification, denitrification, dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium (DNRA), and assimilatory nitrate reduction (ANR). Nitrogen-transformation potential was partitioned across dominant and minor taxa. Nitrospirota and Pseudomonadota were the most abundant classified phyla, whereas Actinomycetota represented only 4% of the community but included Actinomycetes, which showed the highest within-taxon proportion of nitrogen metabolism associated genes. amoABC was assigned only to Nitrosomonas and Nitrososphaerota, whereas denitrification genes were more widely distributed but frequently occurred as partial pathways. nosZ was detected only in the minor phyla Chloroflexota, Acidobacteriota and Myxococcota. DNRA and ANR-associated genes occurred across multiple lineages; nirA in Nitrospira and DNRA-associated nirBD elsewhere within Nitrospirota suggested nitrifier-associated lineages may also encode nitrogen retention potential. Gene-resolved metagenomics identified candidate low-abundance contributors, restricted distributions of genes associated with ammonia oxidation and nitrous oxide reduction, and nitrogen-retention potential not apparent from taxonomic composition alone. Because the study examined DNA-level potential in a single sludge sample, expression, reactor chemistry and longitudinal data are needed to establish pathway activity and operational relevance.

papers.title: Functional Conservation Amid Extreme Divergence in Freshwater SAR11 Hypervariable Region 2
papers.abstract: The Ca. Pelagibacterales order (SAR11) is a ubiquitous bacterioplankton in aquatic ecosystems. The genomes of SAR11 bacteria contain hypervariable region 2 (HVR2), the largest HVR with extreme diversity. Previous studies collectively indicated the enrichment of cell-surface modification genes on HVR2, which have been hypothesized to facilitate phage evasion. However, characterisation of HVR2 has primarily targeted marine clades and been limited for freshwater SAR11 (aka. Fontibacterium). Here, we employed single-cell genomics and recovered 176 Fontibacterium HVR2 sequences from Lake Biwa (Japan) and Lake Zurich (Switzerland), across multiple sampling years for Lake Biwa. Comparative sequence analyses revealed that freshwater HVR2 showed high intra-population diversity and appears to evolve independently of the rest of the genome, mirroring patterns observed in marine counterparts. Nevertheless, highly conserved HVR2 sequence pairs were observed for distinct Fontibacterium species from the two intercontinental habitats, suggesting horizontal transfers of HVR2 with conserved functional configurations across divergent lineages and large spatial scales. Further comparison with 145 marine HVR2 sequences revealed HVR2 sequences displaying synteny between Fontibacterium and marine SAR11, and 209 gene families conserved across habitats, including three near-universally conserved families. All examined freshwater HVR2s contained initiator methionine tRNA genes concentrated near the boundaries of the 5S region, suggesting a tDNA-anchored integration mechanism. These results suggest the functional equivalence of HVR2 across marine and freshwater SAR11 clades, and the existence of a shared pool of HVR2 sequences that evolve reticulately through mutual genetic exchange, independent of the vertical inheritance of the rest of the genome.

papers.title: Parsimonious Creatures: Building Gene Regulatory Networks Robust to Somatic Evolution
papers.abstract: For early multicellular life to have formed and maintained cellular organization, preventing loss of controlled cell replication due to somatic evolution was of critical importance, and remains important to this day for control of cancer. We study how gene regulatory networks (GRNs) can be designed to slow the divergence of somatic clonal lineages in the context of early multicellular life. We model the mutation of GRNs within simplified 12-celled organisms we term "parsimonious creatures", who must replicate from a single cell to 12 cells and then prevent replication past 12 cells to maximize fitness. We found two minimal motifs can achieve these goals, but both are prone to breakdown through somatic evolution: The feedforward motif, which is loosely regulating but relatively robust, and the simple step motif, which uses strong interactions and feedback to form memoryless ultrasensitivity, but is fragile. These simple motifs may be duplicated to form redundant networks via one of two structures: averaging redundancy, which averages multiple sources of information, and min redundancy, which adopts the most conservative source. Averaging redundancy uniformly slows somatic evolution, while min redundancy stalls somatic evolution until neutral mutations accumulate. Either may be superior dependent on life history. However, averaging redundancy slowly increases fitness as the network becomes larger, but large min redundancy networks eventually become "paralyzed", increasing the probability of senescence and reducing fitness. These GRN designs are idealized, yet provide imperfect solutions with fundamental tradeoffs, offering insight as to why somatic evolution remains an incompletely solved problem for multicellular life.

papers.title: Ultra-low-dose same-target combinations control drug resistance across stages
papers.abstract: The emergence of drug resistance continues to limit the long term effectiveness of cancer therapies [1], as tumour cells adapt to therapeutic selective pressure through diverse genetic and non-genetic routes [2,3]. Despite advances in more potent and next generation inhibitors and mechanism based combination therapies [4,5], durable disease control remains difficult to achieve. Here we tested an alternative strategy: combining multiple inhibitors directed against the same oncogenic driver, each at ultra low doses with minimal individual activity, to delay resistance emergence. In epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) driven cancer models, such ultra low dose same target combinations (ULDCs) distributed individually weak perturbations across multiple inhibitors directed against the same target and achieved substantial growth inhibition in vitro and antitumour activity in vivo despite weak effects of the corresponding single agents. Under similar levels of growth inhibition (~50%), single-agent EGFR inhibitors generated resistant outgrowth, whereas a five drug ULDC delayed resistance emergence. Increasing the number of inhibitors further delayed resistance emergence, with no detectable resistant outgrowth observed for combinations containing 8 to 14 inhibitors within the experimental timeframe. The five drug ULDC also retained measurable growth inhibitory activity against gefitinib resistant PC-9/GR cells, and resistant cells arising under five drug ULDC treatment exhibited markedly greater reversibility following drug withdrawal than those arising under single agent treatment. Although pharmacological additivity or synergy may contribute to the collective growth inhibitory effects of ULDCs, the divergent long term resistance outcomes observed under similar levels of growth inhibition indicate that resistance behaviour is not determined by inhibitory strength alone. Instead, our findings support a model in which increasing same target inhibitor diversity progressively constrains the adaptive trajectories available during resistance evolution, while therapeutic perturbation architecture may also influence the stability of resistant states that emerge. More broadly, these findings support the concept of same target collective suppression, in which multiple individually weak perturbations directed against the same target can collectively produce substantial antitumour activity and constrain resistance evolution across multiple stages. We propose that increasing same target inhibitor diversity may restrict accessible adaptive trajectories, while therapeutic perturbation architecture may also influence the stability of resistant states.

papers.title: Why don't transcription factors exploit inter-nucleotide correlations in binding motifs? Evolution of information encoding strategies on DNA
papers.abstract: Transcription factors have been shown to predominantly rely on independent contributions from each position of their target sequence motifs, even though sequence motifs can encode information through correlations among nucleotide positions. As a result, the position-weight matrix, a simple modeling approach that assumes independence among positions, has long since become the dominant model of TF-DNA binding. Why evolution would favor this comparatively simple strategy, known as single locus information (SI), over a correlation-based one remains unaddressed. Here, we use analytical derivations, numerical approaches and evolutionary simulations to show that SI is intrinsically more robust to mutation than correlated (multi-locus) encodings and is therefore indirectly favored under selection for functional transcriptional regulatory networks. At the same time, we show that SI smooths the affinity landscape, ensuring the evolvability of regulatory interactions. We find the same marked bias toward SI in the genetic code, suggesting that the preference for SI is not specific to transcriptional regulation, but may be a general property of biological codes that must reliably store information on DNA in the face of mutational noise.

papers.title: Historical adaptation to transposable element invasions in Drosophila is primarily due to insertions in existing piRNA clusters
papers.abstract: Transposable elements (TEs) are genomic parasites that shift between host species, which may allow them to escape sequence-specific host silencing mechanisms. One such silencing mechanism, the piRNA pathway, is the main line of defense in the germline of animals, and acts through small RNAs targeting specific TE sequences. Though many mechanistic details of this pathway are known, how it evolves to respond to a new transposable element invasion is not. Here, we examine the piRNA-based response to three recently invading TEs in Drosophila simulans, the P-element, Shellder and Spoink. To this end, we assembled genomes of 22 strains, annotated piRNA-producing loci (piRNA clusters) in each strain, and located insertions of the new TEs within these loci. We find that piRNA clusters are highly polymorphic among strains and piRNAs targeting the new TEs come mostly from clusters that likely pre-date the invasions, though there is also some evidence of piRNAs generated de novo, particularly for the long-terminal repeat (LTR) elements. Moreover, resistance to each TE appears to have evolved mostly independently in the different strains through distinct insertions, often in different clusters, although some loci, such as flamenco for Shellder, are recurrent targets.

papers.title: A coral-linked adaptive radiation in butterflyfishes
papers.abstract: Coral reefs harbour a disproportionate share of marine biodiversity, yet whether reef fish diversity reflects steady accumulation or rapid, ecologically driven diversification remains unclear. Butterflyfishes and bannerfishes (Chaetodontidae) include more than half of all coral-feeding fish species, making them a natural test of adaptive radiation on coral reefs. Here we present a time-calibrated phylogeny of 120 of the 138 species, built from 1,009 ultraconserved elements. The species-rich butterflyfishes (Chaetodontinae) are a recent radiation that originated in the Late Miocene (7.78 million years ago; 95% highest posterior density 7.13 to 8.49 million years ago), with much of their extant species diversity arising within the past 2 million years. The crown diversification rate of butterflyfishes is the highest among 29 comparator reef-fish lineages. Ancestral state reconstructions indicate that the ancestor of Chaetodontinae was a facultative corallivore, that a unique jaw joint arose before obligate corallivory, and that obligate corallivory then evolved repeatedly from facultative ancestors, alongside derived tooth morphologies. Together, these results suggest that Late Miocene coral reef turnover and the diversification of branching corals generated an ecological opportunity that functional innovations allowed butterflyfishes to exploit, extending the adaptive radiation framework to open marine seascapes beyond the island and lake systems where it has most often been applied.

papers.title: The structure and evolution of sex chromosomes in an androdioecious species with two mating types.
papers.abstract: Though flowering plants are ancestrally hermaphroditic, some species have evolved sexual specialization and are now composed of individuals expressing just one of their two reproductive functions (either male or female) together with co-sexual individuals. Androdioecy, the co-existence of males with hermaphrodites, is rare across the living world, but unusually common in species of the Oleaceae plant family. The mediterranean shrub Phillyrea angustifolia has a simple mendelian XY sex-determination system for androdioecy, but the underlying molecular determinants and the evolutionary history of the X and Y chromosomes remain unknown. The ability of males to by-pass the self-incompatibility phenotype expressed in hermaphrodites is essential to explain their high frequency in natural populations, but how the loci governing sex and self-incompatibility epistatically interact also remains unknown. To address these questions, we obtained full haplotype-resolved de novo chromosomal assemblies of P. angustifolia and its sister species P. latifolia. The sex-determining region in P. angustifolia spanned a fifth of chromosome 12, and was strikingly larger and more rearranged than that in P. latifolia. The male-specific region contains two putative sex-determining genes, ANDY1 and ANDY2, a tandem encoding two flowering-related transcription factors that arose by translocation followed by duplication of an autosomal gene before the two species diverged. Strikingly, this sex-determining region also contains a recent duplicate of the pollen allergen gene Ole-e1, which shows the strongest differential expression between the two self-incompatibility groups of hermaphrodites, hence establishing a direct molecular link between sex and self-incompatibility. Overall, our results provide novel insight on sex determination and the evolution of sex chromosomes in a plant lineage where the separation between sexes is still incomplete, and offer a possible mechanistic basis for the strong epistatic interaction between the sex and self-incompatibility determinants, with direct implication for how sex-ratios are established in nature.

papers.title: The co-evolution of adhesion and F-actin gives rise to hierarchical cellular force generation
papers.abstract: Cells --- the basic units of life --- dynamically adhere to their micro-environment, build their F-actin cytoskeleton, and apply molecular-motor generated contractile forces to it in a remarkably broad range of biological processes and physiological functions, in both health and disease. Yet, how these processes are orchestrated over multiple spatiotemporal scales is not fully understood. Using several experimental approaches and a theoretical framework, we show that adhesion assembly, on-adhesion F-actin accumulation and the contractile force itself all follow the same time evolution over tens of minutes, the cellular force timescale, at well-defined adhesion sites. We also show that the F-actin distribution away from the adhesion site features a multiplicative space-time decomposition. Finally, we show that F-actin retrograde flow --- central in the so-called molecular motor-clutch models --- is markedly faster than force generation rates, that it does not slow down over maturing adhesions and that its density drops at adhesion sites. These findings suggest a hierarchical, multi- scale force generation process that is controlled by slow adhesion recruitment, which is accompanied by rapid, bursty linear actin polymerization. The linear F-actin slowly accumulates with adhesion recruitment to form an extended near-adhesion F-actin network to which molecular motors attach and apply elastic-like contraction.

papers.title: KAT6 and KAT7 actively maintain mitotic chromatin composition and acetylation to preserve developmental competence
papers.abstract: Mitotic bookmarking enables transmission of regulatory information across cell division, yet how active chromatin states are molecularly preserved during mitosis and how they contribute to postmitotic cell fate decisions remain unresolved. Here, we demonstrate that the acetyltransferases KAT6 and KAT7 remain chromatin-bound and catalytically active throughout mitosis in mouse and human pluripotent stem cells. Acute KAT6/7 depletion disrupts mitotic histone acetylation and the retention of multiple chromatin regulators with minimal effects on chromatin accessibility. Mechanistically, KAT6/7 bookmark both self renewal and developmental gene loci, where they are required for post-mitotic transcriptional reactivation and priming of lineage-specific programs. Consistently, genes impaired during postmitotic reactivation also fail to activate during neuronal differentiation upon continuous KAT6/7 perturbation, compromising the establishment of the neuronal program and identity. Altogether, our findings identify KAT6 and KAT7 as a cooperative mitotic chromatin maintenance system that couples active histone acetylation to preservation of chromatin composition, transcriptional memory, and developmental competence across cell division, extending the bookmarking function beyond transcriptional memory. These findings also provide a new framework for understanding KAT6/7 function in neurodevelopmental disorders and cancer.

papers.title: Expansion and Comprehensive Evaluation of the Peacock Eye Disease Management (PedMan) System across Olive Cultivars Differing in Susceptibility to Venturia oleaginea
papers.abstract: Peacock eye disease, caused by Venturia oleaginea , is an important foliar disease of olive that is primarily managed through fungicide applications. Integrating host resistance into disease-warning systems could improve spray timing and reduce unnecessary fungicide use. PedMan (Peacock eye disease Manager) was previously developed and validated for highly susceptible olive cultivars. The objectives of the present study were to expand PedMan to cultivars differing in susceptibility to V. oleaginea and to evaluate the expanded system under commercial grove conditions. A sensitivity analysis of the rainfall and temperature criteria used for highly susceptible cultivars was conducted to establish criteria for moderately susceptible and moderately resistant cultivars. The rainfall threshold of [≥]15 mm was retained, whereas the temperature range triggering an infection alert was narrowed from 12-18 {degrees}C for highly susceptible cultivars to 13-17 {degrees}C for moderately susceptible and 14-16 {degrees}C for moderately resistant cultivars. The expanded system was subsequently evaluated in 33 field trials and observations under natural infection conditions. PedMan recommendations were classified as correct or incorrect based on statistical comparisons of leaf abscission between fungicide-treated and untreated trees. Overall, 30 of 33 recommendations were correct, resulting in an accuracy of 90.9%. Sensitivity was 87.0%, while specificity and positive predictive value were both 100%. These results demonstrate that incorporating cultivar susceptibility into PedMan broadens its applicability and provides reliable cultivar-specific fungicide recommendations. The system has potential to reduce unnecessary fungicide applications while maintaining effective management of peacock eye disease across olive cultivars differing in susceptibility.

papers.title: Developing a Multimodal miR-15a Mimic to Overcome Gemcitabine and RAS(ON) Inhibitor Daraxonrasib Resistance in Pancreatic Ductal Adenocarcinoma
papers.abstract: Gemcitabine remains a mainstay of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) treatment, while the RAS(ON) inhibitor daraxonrasib has recently demonstrated improved survival in previously treated metastatic disease. However, acquired resistance to both therapies remains a major clinical challenge. Here, we developed MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a, a multimodal microRNA (miRNA)-based therapeutic, by chemically modifying tumor-suppressive miR-15a with methotrexate (MTX), 5-fluorouracil (5-FU), and gemcitabine (Gem) to combine sequence-specific gene regulation with disruption of nucleotide metabolism. MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a exhibited low-nanomolar potency across five PDAC cell lines and retained activity in gemcitabine- and daraxonrasib-resistant models under vehicle-free conditions, substantially exceeding that of stoichiometrically matched free antimetabolites. Treatment induced S-phase accumulation, increased DNA damage and apoptosis, and suppressed checkpoint and survival-associated proteins, including WEE1, CHK1, YAP1, and BCL-2. Transcriptomic and proteomic analyses revealed increased DNA replication, replication-stress, and repair-associated programs, together with reduced oncogenic signaling. In gemcitabine-resistant cells, treatment restored the gemcitabine-activating enzyme dCK, reduced ABCC1 and ABCC3 expression, and suppressed resistance-associated signaling programs, indicating partial remodeling of resistance-associated pathways. MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a also synergized with daraxonrasib (mean Bliss synergy score, 22.52) and activated tumor-cell-intrinsic STING-TBK1 signaling, accompanied by increased interferon stimulated gene expression and IFN-{beta} and CXCL10 secretion. Finally, MTX-5-FU-Gem-miR-15a retained low-nanomolar potency in three patient-derived PDAC organoids and significantly suppressed metastatic tumor growth in vivo at 4 mg/kg. Together, these findings support a multimodal miRNA therapeutic strategy that combines replication-associated DNA damage, checkpoint protein suppression, and innate immune activation-associated responses to target therapeutic resistance in PDAC.

papers.title: Miniaturized Traceless Staudinger Ligation Enables Direct-to-Biology Screening of Potent BRD4 PROTACs
papers.abstract: Direct-to-biology (D2B) approaches accelerate PROTAC discovery by enabling biological screening of crude reaction mixtures without intermediate purification. However, the range of chemical transformations compatible with these workflows remains limited. Herein, we establish a miniaturized, base-free traceless Staudinger ligation platform diversifying linker chemistry for a preexisting library of E3-ligand-linker adducts bearing azide moieties. As a proof-of-concept target, BRD4 was chosen, yielding amide-linked BRD4-targeting PROTACs. By combining phosphine-functionalized JQ1 derivatives with 72 selected azide building blocks, reactions were performed on a 5 L scale in 384-well plates, achieving a mean LC-MS conversion of approximately 65%. Spiking experiments confirmed that the phosphine starting materials had no significant impact on BRD4 degradation, supporting the direct biological evaluation of crude reaction mixtures in the presence of residual starting material. Cellular screening identified 23 hits at 250 nM screening concentration, reducing BRD4 levels below 40%. Two resynthesized and purified PROTACs were subsequently validated, displaying pDC50 values of 8.2 and 7.0 and a Dmax of 90% and 96%, respectively. This work establishes traceless Staudinger ligation as a complementary D2B strategy for the rapid discovery of amide-linked PROTACs.

papers.title: Development of a Thyroid Cancer to Lung Metastasis-on-a-Chip Model
papers.abstract: Background: Study of the metastatic cascade in differentiated non-medullary thyroid cancer (NMTC) is hampered by the relative lack of preclinical models that metastasize from primary tumors to other organs. We previously identified regulator of calcineurin 1 isoform 4 (RCAN1.4) as a suppressor of NMTC cell growth, invasion, and metastasis using in vitro systems and tail vein injections in immunocompromised mice. We then reported a microfluidic device mimicking the mouse tail vein injection where cancer cells were allowed to flow directly to lung organoid constructs. We now report the development of a full primary tumor to lung metastasis-on-a-chip (MOC) model for TC. Methods: Resin molds for primary and secondary sites connected by a channel were 3D printed and filled with polydimethylsiloxane to create a molded silicone elastomer. The primary site was seeded with an organoid composed of a hyaluronic acid and collagen-based hydrogel into which FTC236 and HTh74 NMTC cells with and without knockdown of RCAN1.4 were engrafted. The secondary site consisted of a hydrogel organoid into which bronchial epithelial cells and lung fibroblasts were seeded. Culture media was circulated and movement of NMTC cells to the secondary site was assessed. Results: Both cell lines that expressed RCAN 1.4 metastasized to the secondary lung site. RCAN1.4-reduced FTC236 cells had increased metastatic behavior vs controls while HTh74 was less affected by RCAN1.4 loss, similar to prior studies. To determine if the MOC could be used for incorporation of immune components and therapeutic modeling, NK-92 cells were added and were shown to be reduce metastases for both cell lines in the presence or absence of RCAN1.4. Analysis of MOC circulating fluid revealed elevated levels of granzyme B, consistent with NK-92 cell activation. Cytokine profiling identified elevated probable NMTC and NK-92-derived factors. Conclusions: These results indicate that NMTC metastatic behavior can be modeled using a novel MOC system for mechanistic and preclinical therapeutic studies.

papers.title: Evolutionary games on networks with negative edge-based environmental feedback
papers.abstract: Environmental feedback can fundamentally alter the game payoff structure underlying the evolution of cooperation. How feedback-evolving games interact with population structure under non-weak selection remains incompletely understood. We study an evolutionary game on networks in which each edge has a binary environmental state that determines the payoff matrix used by the two connected individuals. By assumption, cooperation tends to improve the local environment, which in turn favors defection, thereby creating negative feedback between strategies coupled with the environmental condition. We analyze the model under strong selection using a mean-field approximation, a pair approximation that tracks both strategy pairs and edge environments, and agent-based simulations. In well-mixed populations, the feedback can generate bistability between full cooperation and full defection, as well as sustained oscillations arising through a Hopf bifurcation. Sparse networks (i.e., with low nodes' degrees) can eliminate bistability, suppress oscillations, and produce stable intermediate levels of cooperation. The pair approximation captures these effects and generally agrees more closely with simulations on sparse networks than the mean-field approximation. Our results show that edge-based environmental feedback and network structure, such as density of edges, interact to determine whether the fraction of cooperators stabilizes or oscillates over time.

papers.title: Dissecting human embryonic patterning during organogenesis reveals a rostral midline progenitor population for mesoendoderm induction
papers.abstract: Understanding how human organogenesis is accomplished via intricate spatiotemporal patterning of organ primordia requires spatial atlases at cellular resolution. However, existing human embryo spatial atlases are built using sequencing-based platforms such as Stereo-seq, which have limited spatial resolution and blurred anatomical boundaries, leading to misclassification across adjacent cells. Here, we integrate in situ imaging-based transcriptomics (Xenium) with transcriptome-wide spatial profiling (Visium-HD) of Carnegie stages 9-12 embryos to delineate the patterning of core embryonic tissues at single-cell resolution, including the brain, spinal cord, somites, neural crest, notochord, heart, and gut tube. A new finding enabled by spatial single-cell resolution is the identification of rostral midline progenitors (RMPs), a cell population co-expressing SOX2, TBXT, and OTX2. Transcriptionally, RMPs are distinct from both neuromesodermal progenitors (NMPs) and prechordal mesoderm, and in vivo clonal barcoding in mice indicates that RMPs share a common developmental origin with rostral neural ectoderm. To interrogate their functional significance, we leveraged our spatial transcriptome data to recapitulate RMP-like cells from human pluripotent stem cells and showed that these cells can induce epiblast-like cells to acquire mesendodermal and endodermal fates, while themselves adopting an ectodermal fate consistent with their in vivo counterparts. This work provides a 3D, stage-resolved molecular cell atlas of tissue patterning in human embryo that serves as a reference for in vitro models.

papers.title: LuCEMe: An accessible luciferase-based method to functionally assess cellular metabolism across model systems
papers.abstract: Metabolic profiling approaches such as extracellular flux analysis, metabolomics, stable isotope tracing and cytometry-based assays have transformed our understanding of cellular metabolism in physiological and pathological contexts. However, most techniques require specialized equipment or reagents, and do not allow differential metabolic analysis in intact multicellular systems. Here, we present LuCEMe, a luciferase-based metabolic phenotyping approach that combines acute metabolic perturbations with quantitative ATP measurements to resolve glycolytic and mitochondrial dependencies and capacities under native culture conditions, including in complex coculture and ex vivo systems without prior cell separation. The assay can also be adapted to increase metabolic resolution and distinguish between glycolytic activity, glucose oxidation and fatty acid/amino acid-driven mitochondrial ATP production. We use LuCEMe to reveal profound metabolic differences between leukemia cells cocultured with macrophages, stromal cells or adipocytes, and demonstrate distinct metabolic rewiring during macrophage polarization, osteogenic and adipogenic differentiation, and T cell activation. Ex vivo LuCEMe analysis identified a particular metabolic adaptation associated with chemotherapy response in acute myeloid leukemia that was not evident from conventional analyses. LuCEMe thus provides an accessible, robust and versatile framework for direct functional metabolic phenotyping across in vitro, ex vivo, and multicellular systems that complements existing metabolic profiling technologies.

papers.title: Homogeneous network inference for subtype-stratified master regulator analysis in cancer
papers.abstract: Master-regulator analysis of 34 TCGA tumour cohorts (cancer x molecular subtype; n between 27 and 562 tumours) requires one regulatory network per cohort. Mutual-information (MI) networks inferred with ARACNe3 are the usual choice, but they are not available for the smallest cohorts; filling the gap with correlation networks would mix two methods inside the very comparison between subtypes that the analysis is meant to make. We therefore infer every network with a single procedure, fixed-size Spearman regulons (FSR): rank correlation between regulator and target, a fixed effect-size threshold rho >= 0.2, the per-target data-processing-inequality (DPI) pruning implemented in corto, bootstrap support, and truncation to the 100 best-supported targets per regulator. We quantify what this choice concedes and what it provides, labelling each claim as a standard result, a heuristic, or an empirical result. Rank correlation is more powerful than the MI estimators we simulated for n = 95) they overlap in 0.7 of the top-20 regulators, the same as two filterings of the same ARACNe3 network, although the rank correlation of the full score vector shows a measurable method effect in the tail. Subsampling large real cohorts indicates that networks inferred from fewer than 60 tumours do not reliably reproduce their own cohort's master regulators, that 60-100 is a grey zone, and that a cancer-wide network does not rescue small subtypes. We present FSR as an adequate and uniform choice for multi-cohort analysis, not as a statistically superior one.

papers.title: Melanoidins Suppress Cucumber and Tomato Diseases Incited by Pathogens that are Oomycetes, Bacteria and a Virus
papers.abstract: We recently reported that solutions of the nitrogenous compounds melanoidins (M), that are formed during the final stages of the Maillard Reaction, are inducers of plant resistance (Elad et al. 2026). M promoted immunity and induced disease resistance through an effect on the transcriptome, primarily through the salicylic acid pathway. Here we tested the effect of M on plant diseases that are caused by Oomycetes, bacteria and a tobamovirus. Drench and spray of M suppressed Pythium aphanidermatum damping off in cucumber, cucumber downy mildew (Pseudoperonospera cubensis), tomato late blight (Phytophthora infestans), bacterial speck (Pseudomonas syringae pv. tomato), bacterial canker (Clavibacter michiganensis subsp. michiganensis) and the Tobamovirus Tomato brown rugose fruit virus (ToBRFV) in tomato. In various experiments control was achieved by concentrations of 0.03 and 0.1% and on older and younger leaves and even in long term experiments where the M was applied for ca 11 weeks. It can be concluded that the disease resistance inducer M can suppress soilborne and foliar diseases that are caused by Oomycetes, bacteria and a virus of the genus Tobamovirus, in addition to the fungal pathogen Botrytis cinerea reported earlier.

papers.title: A distinct chondrogenic progenitor population from human umbilical cord derived mesenchymal stromal cells for osteoarthritis therapy
papers.abstract: Stem cell-based cartilage regeneration remains constrained by functional heterogeneity and phenotypic drift in conventional cell sources, compromising durable structural repair. Human umbilical cord-derived mesenchymal stromal cells (UC-MSCs) represent an accessible, off-the-shelf cell source; however, their broad clinical utility is hampered by cellular heterogeneity, leaving the key chondrogenic subpopulation responsible for cartilage repair unresolved. By integrating single-cell transcriptomics with functional assays, we identified and prospectively isolated a distinct, highly expandable subpopulation of skeletal stem cell-like progenitors (U-CPCs) from the human umbilical cord, establishing an extra-skeletal cell source uniquely primed for joint restoration. Single-cell transcriptomics reveal their inherent regulatory landscape, uncovering a distinct transcriptional state uniquely primed for chondrogenesis. In comparison with conventional stem cells and other tissue-derived SSC-like populations (from umbilical cord, bone marrow, adipose tissue, and dental pulp), U-CPCs exhibit a markedly enhanced chondrogenic capacity. In both a mouse cartilage injury model and a rat osteoarthritis model, the administration of U-CPCs effectively mitigates joint degeneration and drives the restoration of a structurally sound, hyaline-like matrix. Mechanistically, U-CPCs secrete extracellular vesicles enriched with microRNA Let-7a-5p, which specifically modulates DUSP7/MAPK/ERK signaling in recipient chondrocytes, thereby restoring extracellular matrix homeostasis and promoting cartilage repair. By characterizing these specialized extra-skeletal progenitors and elucidating both their intrinsic chondrogenic priming and paracrine regulation of host tissue, this study establishes U-CPCs as a robust, lineage-restricted cellular source for osteoarthritis therapy.

papers.title: EWSR1::ATF1 hyperactivation via TRIM11 depletion triggers lethal metabolic rewiring in clear cell sarcoma
papers.abstract: Clear cell sarcoma (CCS) is an ultra-rare and aggressive soft tissue sarcoma driven by the EWSR1::ATF1 fusion oncoprotein. Currently, no effective and well-tolerated treatment options are available to CCS patients. Direct inhibition of fusion transcription factors is precluded by the absence of defined ligand-binding pockets, whereas their abundance is under the control of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), offering an alternative avenue for biology-guided treatment. Here we show the abundance of EWSR1::ATF1 is tightly regulated by the UPS, and that release of this constraint is lethal to CCS cells. A reporter-based CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screen of UPS components identified TRIM11 as an E3 ligase that regulates turnover of EWSR1::ATF1, which it recognises as a neosubstrate without altering wild-type EWSR1 or ATF1. Depletion of TRIM11 increased nuclear fusion protein abundance, amplified the fusion-driven transcriptional programs and reduced viability. Proteomic analysis identified the cataplerotic enzyme phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1 (PCK1), a direct EWSR1::ATF1 target, as the key mediator of lethal effects of fusion hyperactivation. Extracellular flux analysis, isotope tracing and quantitative metabolomics revealed excessive cataplerotic carbon withdrawal and impaired oxidative phosphorylation as the underlying mechanism. In patient tumors, high PCK1 expression associated with metastatic transcriptome programs and disease presentation, as well as shorter survival. Taken together, we report that hyperactivation of EWSR1::ATF1 opens a metabolic vulnerability, establishing TRIM11 as an actionable dependency and PCK1 as a candidate prognostic biomarker in CCS.

papers.title: Protecting host mitochondria with vitamin B3 preserves bioenergetics and thermogenesis during antibiotic treatment
papers.abstract: Antibiotics that target bacterial translation can also impair mitochondrial function because mitochondria retain bacterial-like ribosomes. As antibiotic resistance continues to increase and the use of several broad-spectrum antibiotics has been limited by their mitochondrial toxicity, there is a growing need to understand their off-target effects in host physiology, and to identify strategies that can mitigate antibiotic-induced mitochondrial dysfunction. We demonstrate that antibiotic chloramphenicol (CA) induces a dose-dependent reduction in mitochondrial respiration and mitochondrial thermogenesis in Drosophila S2 cells, human HEK293T cells and in developing Drosophila larvae. In vivo, CA exposure triggers female-biased aberrant innate immune activation of hosts carrying naturally occurring mitochondrial rRNA variants. Metabolomic profiling revealed alterations in vitamin B3 metabolism in Drosophila during and following CA exposure. Among the vitamin B3 vitamers examined, nicotinamide (NAM) exhibited the strongest protective effect, mitigating the CA-induced impairments in mitochondrial respiration and thermogenesis, as well as aberrant immune activation. We identify mitochondrial thermogenesis as a previously unrecognized target of antibiotic-induced mitochondrial perturbation and a sensitive marker of mitochondrial stress. Furthermore, we demonstrate that co-supplementation of CA with NAM mitigates antibiotic-induced mitochondrial toxicity through evolutionarily conserved mitochondrial pathways. Finally, we establish Drosophila as a powerful model for investigating antibiotic-induced mitochondrial dysfunction and for developing therapeutic strategies to protect host mitochondria during antibiotic treatment.

papers.title: A global post-transcriptional regulator directs Acinetobacter baumannii carbon preference and gut colonization
papers.abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a multidrug-resistant pathogen that colonizes the gut, increasing the risk of subsequent infection and transmission. Recent work showed that A. baumannii catabolizes ornithine, a non-preferred carbon source, to colonize the gut. However, the mechanisms of carbon preference were unknown in A. baumannii. Here, experimental evolution identified the conserved RNA-binding protein CsrA as a regulator of carbon preference in A. baumannii, a previously unreported CsrA function. RNA immunoprecipitation sequencing (RIP-Seq) revealed hundreds of CsrA-associated transcripts. A. baumannii CsrA directly bound and repressed expression of the ast arginine/ornithine catabolic operons. The Pseudomonas aeruginosa CsrA homolog RsmA repressed arginine/ornithine catabolic operon expression, suggesting this CsrA function extends to other bacterial taxa. Finally, CsrA was required for competitive fitness during A. baumannii gut colonization. These findings uncover a previously unrecognized role for a global regulator in A. baumannii carbon preference and persistence in the gut, a critical reservoir for multidrug-resistant pathogens.

papers.title: Alveolar and airway progenitors converge on an epigenetically encoded profibrotic state
papers.abstract: During organ regeneration, epithelial transitional states arise from progenitors and instruct the mesenchyme to remodel the extracellular matrix. However, the identity of the progenitors, the mechanisms underlying this transition, and why these states persist in tissue fibrosis often remain elusive. Here, using lineage tracing in mice, we show that the profibrotic KRT5-/KRT17+ state in pulmonary fibrosis arises convergently from alveolar type (AT) 2 and airway secretory cells. AT1 cells generate neither KRT5-/KRT17+ nor AT2 cells. TGF-{beta}/SMAD3 acts through KMT2A and p300 to epigenetically reprogram human AT2 cells into the KRT5-/KRT17+ state. In human pulmonary fibrosis, KRT5-/KRT17+ cells slough off, and transitional cells re-epithelialize the denuded basement membrane. Transcriptionally convergent states arise in injured kidney, skin, and intestine. This work reframes fibrogenesis as the accumulation of a conserved profibrotic transitional state via ongoing turnover, not persistence alone, and nominates the state transition and its epigenetic regulators as therapeutic targets.
